name: Maryland
dueDateNotes: Maryland follows the federal schedule: April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15. If a due date falls on a weekend or holiday, it moves to the next business day.
selfEmploymentNotes: Maryland taxes your federal AGI after a flat standard deduction ($3,350 single / $6,700 married for 2025) at graduated rates from 2% to 6.5%; 2025 added new top brackets of 6.25% (over $500,000 single / $600,000 married) and 6.50% (over $1 million / $1.2 million). Crucially, every Maryland county and Baltimore City adds its own local income tax on the same income — 2.25% to 3.30% in 2025 — which this calculator includes and pre-fills at 3.20%, editable to your county's rate.
uniqueFacts: Maryland is the only state where every county and Baltimore City levies its own local income tax — 2.25% to 3.30% in 2025 — on top of the state income tax.
Maryland's county tax is charged on the same income as the state tax and is often close to half of the state portion, so your quarterly estimates must cover state and local together.
Maryland added two new high-income brackets for 2025 under the Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act: 6.25% (over $500,000 single / $600,000 joint) and 6.50% (over $1 million / $1.2 million joint).

extraFaqs.q: What local income tax rate does my Maryland county charge?
extraFaqs.a: Every Maryland county and Baltimore City sets its own 2025 local income tax rate on the same income the state taxes, per the Comptroller's estimated-tax (Form PV) worksheet: 3.30% in Dorchester; 3.20% in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Calvert, Caroline, Howard, Kent, Montgomery, Prince George's, Queen Anne's, St. Mary's, Somerset, and Wicomico; 3.06% in Harford; 3.03% in Allegany, Carroll, and Charles; 2.95% in Washington; 2.74% in Cecil; 2.65% in Garrett; 2.40% in Talbot; and 2.25% in Worcester. Anne Arundel and Frederick use graduated local brackets (roughly 2.7% to 3.2%), so the single editable rate here is an approximation for those two. The calculator pre-fills 3.20% — the rate most Marylanders pay — but change the 'Your county rate' box to match your county.

extraFaqs.q: How does Maryland's standard deduction and personal exemption work?
extraFaqs.a: For 2025 Maryland switched to a flat standard deduction of $3,350 (single) or $6,700 (married filing jointly), replacing the older rule that set it at 15% of your income capped at a few thousand dollars. Maryland also gives a $3,200 personal exemption per person, which this calculator does not subtract — so its estimate runs slightly high, a deliberately conservative cushion. That exemption phases out for higher earners (above roughly $100,000 single / $150,000 married), which is why we leave it out rather than guess your phase-out.

extraFaqs.q: Does this include Maryland's capital gains surcharge?
extraFaqs.a: No. Maryland's 2025 law added a 2% surcharge on certain high-income capital gains, but this calculator models only ordinary self-employment income and does not apply a capital-gains surtax. If a large share of your income is investment gains, your actual Maryland tax could be higher than shown.

extraFaqs.q: Do I have to make Maryland estimated payments, and what's the safe harbor?
extraFaqs.a: Maryland requires estimated payments once you expect to owe more than $500 in state and local tax after withholding (Comptroller Form PV worksheet; COMAR 03.04.01.02). To avoid a penalty, pay either 90% of this year's Maryland tax or 110% of last year's — and Maryland applies the 110% prior-year figure at every income level, with no lower 100% tier for modest incomes like the federal rules have.

extraFaqs.q: What if I win a prize or lottery money in Maryland?
extraFaqs.a: Maryland treats large winnings specially: if you receive $500 or more of prize or gambling income, you must file a declaration of estimated tax and pay it in full within 60 days, rather than waiting for the next regular quarterly due date.
